reigns.tagline: He made China one country and still feared death
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of King Zhuangxiang of Qin
reigns.previously: Seven kingdoms have fought each other for 250 years. Qin is winning.
paragraphs: For two and a half centuries, the Warring States, seven kingdoms had battled over China. Qin, the hard state in the west, ran on harsh laws, farming and war. Its king, Ying Zheng, took the throne as a boy in 246 BC. In 227 BC an assassin, Jing Ke, came to court to present a map. Rolled up inside was a poisoned dagger. The king dodged round a pillar until he could tug out his long sword. Then Qin swallowed the other six kingdoms one by one.

In 221 BC he made up a new title, huangdi, "emperor", and called himself the First. With his minister Li Si he pressed the old kingdoms into one mould: one script, one coin (round with a square hole), the same weights and measures, even the same axle widths for carts. He linked older walls into a long northern wall and built roads and canals. In 213 BC he had books burned, and the next year scholars were said to be buried alive.

He was terrified of dying. He sent the magician Xu Fu out to sea to find the elixir of life, and Xu Fu never came back. The emperor died on tour in 210 BC. His chief eunuch Zhao Gao and Li Si hid the death, and a forged order told his eldest son, Fusu, to kill himself. Fusu obeyed. Under a hill near Xi'an, the emperor's tomb was guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

claims.text: He burned the books and buried 460 scholars alive.
claims.note: The story comes from Sima Qian, writing a century later under the Han, who needed Qin to look monstrous. The book burning is widely accepted; the live burial is doubted by many modern historians.

claims.text: He sent Xu Fu with thousands of young men and women across the sea to find the elixir of life.
claims.note: Sima Qian records the voyage. The later tale that Xu Fu landed in Japan and stayed has no evidence behind it.

claims.text: Farmers digging a well in 1974 found the Terracotta Army.
claims.note: The discovery near Xi'an is well documented; excavation has gone on ever since, and the tomb mound itself is still unopened.

reigns.hook: The First Emperor is dead in a closed carriage, and only a handful of men know. To hide the smell, a cart of salted fish rolls along beside it. Back in the capital, a younger son is about to become emperor.

reigns.title: The Fall of Qin
reigns.tagline: A deer called a horse, and an empire in flames
reigns.reignEnded: Xiang Yu dies at the Wu River
reigns.previously: The First Emperor is dead, and a forged order has killed his heir.
paragraphs: The plotters made the younger son Huhai the Second Emperor. The real power was the eunuch Zhao Gao. One day he brought a deer to court and called it a horse. Courtiers who said "deer" were noted down and later destroyed. Meanwhile the Qin laws ground on. In 209 BC two conscript leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, were held up by rain. Late meant death under Qin law, they reasoned, so they might as well rebel. China caught fire.

Zhao Gao had Li Si cut in half in 208 BC, then forced Huhai to kill himself. The next ruler, Ziying, stabbed Zhao Gao and surrendered to the rebel Liu Bang in 207 BC. Then Xiang Yu of Chu arrived, a towering aristocrat and the best fighter of the age. He massacred Ziying's family and burned the capital, Xianyang. At a feast at Hongmen his adviser had a sword dance staged to kill Liu Bang, who slipped out to the latrine and fled.

Xiang Yu carved up the empire, sent Liu Bang to the remote land of Han, and the two fought for four years. In 202 BC Xiang Yu was trapped at Gaixia. At night he heard the songs of Chu coming from the enemy camp and thought his homeland had gone over. He sang a farewell to his beloved Lady Yu, broke out with a few horsemen, and killed himself on the bank of the Wu River.

claims.text: Zhao Gao called a deer a horse to see who dared contradict him.
claims.note: It's in Sima Qian and became a Chinese idiom for twisting the truth. Nobody can check it, and it fits the Han picture of Qin as rotten.

claims.text: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rebelled because being late meant death under Qin law.
claims.note: That's Sima Qian's version. Qin legal texts found at Shuihudi set fines, not death, for late labour service, though these men were soldiers.

claims.text: Lady Yu killed herself after Xiang Yu's farewell song.
claims.note: Sima Qian gives the song but not her death. Her suicide comes from later writers and was made famous by the opera Farewell My Concubine.

reigns.hook: Liu Bang, a village official who once drank on credit, is the last man standing. A peasant has won the empire. Now he has to work out how to run it.

reigns.tagline: The village constable who founded a dynasty
reigns.previously: Xiang Yu is dead at the Wu River. Liu Bang is the last man standing.
paragraphs: Liu Bang was a farmer's son who became a village constable in Pei. He was loud, lazy, generous and popular, and he drank at the local taverns on credit. In 202 BC he became the first commoner to found a Chinese dynasty. He called it Han, after the land Xiang Yu had fobbed him off with, and built a new capital at Chang'an.

He kept Qin's machinery of government but softened its savage laws. When he first entered the Qin heartland he had promised just three: no murder, no wounding, no theft. He trusted few of his old comrades. The greatest general of the war, Han Xin, was lured into the palace by Gaozu's wife, Empress Lü, and executed in 196 BC.

In 200 BC Gaozu marched north against the Xiongnu, the horse nomads of the steppe, and was surrounded at Baideng for seven days. He got out, and never tried again. Instead he began heqin: brides called princesses and yearly gifts of silk, wine and grain to buy peace. In 195 BC he was hit by an arrow fighting the rebel Ying Bu. When the wound turned bad he sent the doctor away, saying his fate lay with Heaven, and died.

claims.text: Tavern keepers let him drink on credit, then tore up his debts after seeing a dragon hovering over him.
claims.note: Sima Qian tells it. Stories of omens around a founder's youth were standard, and this one was written under his own dynasty.

claims.text: He promised the people of Qin a law code of just three articles.
claims.note: Sima Qian reports the promise, but Han law codes found at Zhangjiashan show the Han soon kept most of the Qin rules.

claims.text: He escaped Baideng by bribing the Xiongnu ruler's wife.
claims.note: Sima Qian says the adviser Chen Ping sent gifts to the chanyu's consort. The plan itself was kept secret, which invited later guesses.

reigns.hook: Gaozu is dead and his heir is a gentle boy of 15. The real power now belongs to the widow, Empress Lü, and she has a long list of scores to settle.

reigns.title: Empress Dowager Lü
reigns.tagline: The first woman to rule China, and the most feared
reigns.cameToPower: Ruled through her son Emperor Hui
reigns.reignEnded: Died; her clan was wiped out
reigns.previously: Gaozu dies of an arrow wound. His teenage son becomes Emperor Hui.
paragraphs: Lü Zhi had married Liu Bang when he was nobody, and spent two years as Xiang Yu's hostage during the war. As empress she helped him destroy the generals he feared. When he died she put her son on the throne as Emperor Hui and ran the empire herself. She was the first woman to rule China in all but name.

She had not forgotten Lady Qi, Gaozu's favourite, who had tried to get her own son Ruyi made heir. Ruyi was poisoned. Lady Qi had her hands and feet cut off, her eyes put out and her ears burned, and was thrown into a privy as the "human swine". Emperor Hui was taken to see her. He wept, fell ill, said he could no longer rule, and drank his life away until he died in 188 BC.

Empress Lü then put two boy emperors on the throne in turn and ruled through them. She broke Gaozu's rule that only his own Liu clan could be kings and made her Lü relatives kings too. A new dynasty seemed to be growing inside the old one. When she died in 180 BC, Gaozu's old generals and the Liu princes struck. They killed the Lü clan, young and old.

claims.text: She turned Lady Qi into the "human swine".
claims.note: Sima Qian tells it in full, writing about a century later under emperors descended from the men who destroyed the Lü clan.

claims.text: Seeing Lady Qi broke Emperor Hui and he gave up governing.
claims.note: Sima Qian says so, and Hui did leave power to his mother. The direct cause is the historian's reading.

claims.text: Her government was good for ordinary people.
claims.note: Even Sima Qian, who told the horror stories, ended her annals saying the empire was at peace, punishments were rare and harvests plentiful.

reigns.hook: The Lü are dead and the throne is empty. The generals want someone harmless. They pick a son of Gaozu by a minor wife, whose mother's family is too weak to cause trouble.

reigns.title: Emperors Wen and Jing
reigns.tagline: Two thrifty emperors and forty quiet years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Wen: son of Gaozu by a minor wife
reigns.previously: Empress Lü is dead and the generals have wiped out her whole clan.
paragraphs: The generals picked Liu Heng because his mother's family was too weak to be a threat. As Emperor Wen he became the model ruler later Confucians dreamed about. He cut the land tax, for years to nothing at all. He wore plain clothes and dropped plans for a new terrace when told it would cost as much as ten ordinary families owned. Father and son between them made "the rule of Wen and Jing" a byword for good government.

In 167 BC a girl named Chunyu Tiying wrote to the emperor. Her father, a doctor, faced mutilation as a punishment, and she offered to become a government slave to spare him. Wen was moved and abolished mutilating punishments. His son, Emperor Jing, took over in 157 BC and kept the thrift going.

Jing had a harder edge. As a prince he had killed a cousin, the heir of the kingdom of Wu, with a game board after a quarrel. In 154 BC that boy's father and six other kings rose in the Rebellion of the Seven States. To calm them, Jing had his own adviser Chao Cuo, who had urged cutting the kings down, executed in his court robes. The rebels fought on anyway and were crushed within three months.

claims.text: Wen was so frugal that he wore coarse clothes and wouldn't spend money on buildings.
claims.note: Sima Qian praises his thrift, but Wen also gave a favourite, Deng Tong, a copper mountain and the right to mint coins.

claims.text: A girl's letter made Wen abolish mutilation.
claims.note: The abolition in 167 BC is real. The tidy story of the dutiful daughter, told by Sima Qian, may have been polished in the retelling.

claims.text: As a prince, Jing killed his cousin with a game board.
claims.note: Sima Qian gives it as the root of the Wu king's grudge. It's the only account, and it serves to explain the rebellion.

reigns.hook: Jing dies in 141 BC. The new emperor is 15 and has no intention of being thrifty. He's going to spend that treasury on armies, horses and the far west.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who pushed China west
reigns.previously: Wen and Jing leave a calm empire and a treasury full to bursting.
paragraphs: Emperor Wu reigned for 54 years, a record no Chinese emperor beat for about 1,800 years. He made Confucian learning the official creed of the state and in 124 BC founded an Imperial Academy to train officials in the classics. Then he went to war. In 138 BC he sent Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu. Zhang Qian was captured and held ten years, escaped, and came home in 126 BC with news of kingdoms China had never heard of.

His generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drove the Xiongnu deep into the steppe, opening the road that became the Silk Road. He fought a war for the "heavenly horses" of Ferghana and conquered lands in Korea, the far south and the south-west. To pay for it all he took over the salt and iron trades. In 99 BC the historian Sima Qian defended a defeated general, Li Ling, and was castrated for it. He lived on to finish his great history, the Shiji.

Old and suspicious, Wu came to believe witchcraft was being used against him. In 91 BC the hunt reached the crown prince, Liu Ju, who was framed and rose in desperation. He lost, and killed himself; so did his mother, the empress. Wu then issued the Luntai edict, regretting the cost of his wars. He died in 87 BC and left the throne to a small boy.

claims.text: Sima Qian chose castration over death so he could finish his history.
claims.note: He says so himself in his Letter to Ren An, preserved in the Hanshu.

claims.text: Ferghana's "heavenly horses" sweated blood.
claims.note: Han writers said so. If it was real, a skin parasite that makes horses bleed is the usual modern guess.

claims.text: In the Luntai edict, Wu publicly apologised for his wars.
claims.note: The text survives in Ban Gu's Hanshu. Some historians think Ban Gu shaped it to make Wu look repentant.

reigns.hook: Emperor Wu dies in 87 BC. The new emperor is a small boy, and a tough general named Huo Guang is left in charge. He will make and unmake emperors.

reigns.title: Regents and In-Laws
reigns.tagline: Regents, in-laws and a 27-day emperor
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir as Wu lay dying
reigns.previously: Emperor Wu dies after 54 years, leaving a small boy on the throne.
paragraphs: The regent Huo Guang ran the empire for the boy Emperor Zhao. When Zhao died young in 74 BC, Huo picked a grandson of Wu, Liu He, then threw him out 27 days later for 1,127 misdeeds. Liu He lived on as a minor marquis. His tomb near Nanchang, dug from 2011, was full of gold and about ten tonnes of bronze coins.

Huo's next pick was Emperor Xuan, grandson of the doomed crown prince Liu Ju. He had survived the witchcraft purge as a baby in prison and grew up a commoner. Xuan bided his time. After Huo Guang died, his family plotted and Xuan wiped them out. Under his son, in 33 BC, the palace lady Wang Zhaojun went north as a bride to the Xiongnu ruler, one of the most famous women in Chinese stories.

Weak emperors followed. The Empress Dowager Wang Zhengjun lived for decades and her Wang relatives took the top jobs. Emperor Ai made his young favourite Dong Xian commander of the armies. Her nephew Wang Mang rose as the perfect Confucian: modest, generous, devoted to ritual. When the boy Emperor Ping died in AD 6, Wang Mang became regent for a toddler, Ruzi Ying. In January of AD 9 he took the throne himself.

claims.text: Liu He was deposed for 1,127 misdeeds in 27 days.
claims.note: The charge sheet is in Ban Gu's Hanshu. It was drawn up by Huo Guang, the man who had just removed him.

claims.text: Emperor Ai cut off his own sleeve rather than wake Dong Xian, asleep on it.
claims.note: The Hanshu tells it; "the passion of the cut sleeve" became a polite phrase for love between men.

claims.text: Wang Mang poisoned Emperor Ping.
claims.note: Rebels against Wang Mang said so. The Hanshu only reports the rumour, and Ping was a sickly boy.

reigns.hook: Wang Mang has the throne and a plan. He will tear up the old Han world and rebuild a lost golden age, starting with who owns the land and what money is.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who tried to rebuild a golden age
reigns.previously: Wang Mang, the model Confucian regent, has taken the Han throne.
paragraphs: Wang Mang named his dynasty Xin, "New", the only break in four centuries of Han rule. He wanted to bring back the perfect age of the ancient Zhou kings. He declared all land to belong to the throne, to be shared out fairly, and banned the buying and selling of slaves. He changed the money again and again, and as regent he had already brought out bronze coins shaped like knives. Each change wiped out people's savings.

Then nature turned on him. Around AD 11 the Yellow River burst its banks and swung onto a new course, drowning farmland and sending crowds of refugees across the north. Famine bred rebels. The Red Eyebrows painted their brows red to tell friend from foe. The Lülin, the "Green Forest" bands, rallied around princes of the old Han family.

In AD 23 Wang Mang sent a huge army against them. At Kunyang a Han prince, Liu Xiu, broke it with a small force as a storm burst over the field. In October rebels stormed Chang'an. Wang Mang was killed in the palace, still clutching his ritual knife and reciting from the classics. His head was hung up in the market for the crowd to pelt.

claims.text: At Kunyang Liu Xiu routed an army of 420,000 men, helped by a storm.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu's numbers are huge and the storm is dramatic; both may be inflated in honour of the man who became emperor.

claims.text: Wang Mang's head was kept in the imperial treasury for over 270 years.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says it was lost in a palace fire in 295, along with Gaozu's sword and Confucius's shoes. Nobody can check it now.

claims.text: He nationalised all land and freed the slaves.
claims.note: The orders were real, but they were watered down or cancelled within three years. How far they were ever carried out is unclear.

reigns.hook: Wang Mang is dead and the Han are back, sort of. Rival princes and rebel armies fight over the ruins, and the hero of Kunyang is quietly building an army of his own.

reigns.tagline: The farmer prince who glued the Han back together
reigns.previously: Wang Mang is dead and the Han princes are fighting over the ruins.
paragraphs: Liu Xiu was a distant Han kinsman, a gentleman farmer who had studied in Chang'an. After Kunyang he served the Gengshi Emperor, another Han prince, who held Chang'an from 23 to 25 until the Red Eyebrows overran it and killed him. By then Liu Xiu had his own army in the north. In 25 he declared himself emperor and moved the capital east to Luoyang. That's why his line is called the Eastern, or Later, Han.

It took him over ten years to put the empire back together. The last big rival, Gongsun Shu in Chengdu, fell in 36. In the far south two sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, led a revolt in what is now Vietnam in 40. Guangwu's general Ma Yuan crushed it by 43. The sisters are still national heroes in Vietnam.

At home Guangwu freed many slaves, shrank the army and lightened taxes. He kept his old comrades-in-arms rich and honoured, but gave the real work of government to officials, so none of them could turn on him. In 57 he sent a gold seal to the king of Na in Japan. A gold seal found by a farmer in Kyushu in 1784 is thought to be that very gift. He died the same year.

claims.text: The gold seal found in Kyushu in 1784 is the one Guangwu sent.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu records the gift in 57, and the seal's wording fits. A few scholars have questioned whether the seal is genuine.

claims.text: He kept his generals rich but out of power, so none could rebel.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu praises him for it. In fact several old comrades did hold office; the policy was looser than the legend.

claims.text: The Trưng sisters drowned themselves rather than surrender.
claims.note: That's the Vietnamese tradition. The Chinese sources say Ma Yuan captured and beheaded them.

reigns.hook: Guangwu leaves a restored empire to his son. Within a few reigns, though, the throne will belong to children, and the palace to their mothers' families and the eunuchs who serve them.

reigns.title: The Later Han Emperors
reigns.tagline: Paper, earthquakes, eunuchs and a yellow sky
reigns.previously: Guangwu dies at Luoyang, leaving the Han restored, his son in charge.
paragraphs: Emperor Ming (57 to 75) dreamed of a golden man flying over his palace. Told it was the Buddha, he sent envoys west, and they came back with monks and scriptures on a white horse. Luoyang's White Horse Temple is said to mark the spot. In Central Asia, Ban Chao won back the oasis cities. His brother Ban Gu wrote the history of the Former Han, and their sister Ban Zhao finished it, China's first famous woman historian.

These were inventive years. In 105 the eunuch Cai Lun presented paper to the throne, and in 132 Zhang Heng built a bronze vessel that sensed distant earthquakes. But the emperors were now mostly children. Their mothers' families and the palace eunuchs fought over them. The general Liang Ji poisoned the boy Emperor Zhi in 146 for calling him an "overbearing general". In 159 Emperor Huan used his eunuchs to destroy Liang Ji.

The eunuchs then ran the court and banned their scholarly critics from office in the Partisan Prohibitions. Emperor Ling (168 to 189) sold official posts for cash. In 184 the faith healer Zhang Jue launched the Yellow Turban rebellion, preaching that the blue sky was dead and a yellow sky would rise. The rebels were beaten, but the generals who beat them now had armies of their own. Ling died in 189.

claims.text: Buddhism came to China after Emperor Ming dreamed of a golden man.
claims.note: The story appears in later Buddhist texts and the Hou Hanshu. Buddhism was probably already trickling in along the trade routes.

claims.text: Cai Lun invented paper.
claims.note: He presented an improved paper in 105, but older paper from the Western Han has been dug up, for example at Fangmatan.

claims.text: Liang Ji had the eight-year-old Emperor Zhi poisoned for calling him overbearing.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so, written long after by historians who saw Liang Ji as the arch-villain. The boy did die suddenly.

reigns.hook: Emperor Ling is dead and the court explodes. Eunuchs murder a general, soldiers massacre the eunuchs, and a frontier warlord named Dong Zhuo marches into Luoyang and grabs the boy emperor.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of a eunuch's adopted son
reigns.cameToPower: Took the emperor into his care
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Luoyang, King of Wei
reigns.previously: Dong Zhuo grabs the boy emperor, burns Luoyang and is killed by Lü Bu.
paragraphs: After Emperor Ling died, the eunuchs murdered the general He Jin, and his men slaughtered the eunuchs. The warlord Dong Zhuo seized the boy Emperor Xian, burned Luoyang in 190 and dragged the court west. In 192 his adopted son Lü Bu killed him. The emperor drifted, half starved, among feuding warlords. In 196 Cao Cao, a sharp and ruthless general, brought him to his own base at Xu and gave orders to the empire in his name.

Cao Cao's great rival was Yuan Shao, master of the north. In 200 Cao beat him at Guandu by raiding and burning his supply depot. In 208 he sailed down the Yangtze to finish off the south, but Sun Quan and Liu Bei beat him at the Red Cliffs, sending fire ships into his fleet. China was now split three ways.

He became chancellor, then King of Wei in 216, but never took the throne. He was also a fine poet, and his verses are still learned today. The 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms made him its scheming villain, and the stage gave him a white face. In 2009 archaeologists announced they had found his tomb near Anyang. He died at Luoyang in March 220.

claims.text: Cao Cao said, "I'd rather betray the world than let the world betray me."
claims.note: It comes from a later anecdote collection quoted by Pei Songzhi in his notes to the Sanguozhi; the novel made it famous.

claims.text: He lost at the Red Cliffs to a fire-ship attack.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi's accounts are brief and differ. Some mention fire, others blame disease in Cao's army; the novel's details are invented.

claims.text: The tomb found near Anyang in 2009 is Cao Cao's.
claims.note: Chinese archaeologists announced it with confidence, but critics have questioned the finds and the identification of the bones.

reigns.hook: Cao Cao dies a king, but not an emperor. His son Cao Pi won't wait. Before the year is out, the last Han emperor will be politely made to hand over the throne.

reigns.title: The Three Kingdoms
reigns.tagline: Three emperors, one empire, and a legend that never ends
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cao Pi, son of Cao Cao
reigns.previously: Cao Cao dies King of Wei. His son Cao Pi has his eye on the throne.
paragraphs: In December 220 Cao Pi made Emperor Xian give up the throne and founded the Wei dynasty. Four centuries of Han were over. Liu Bei, who claimed Han royal blood, declared himself emperor of Shu Han in Chengdu in 221. Sun Quan in the south-east became king of Wu in 222 and emperor in 229. China had three emperors, and each said he was the real one.

Liu Bei's sworn brother Guan Yu had been killed by Wu in 220. Liu Bei attacked Wu for revenge, was beaten, and died at Baidicheng in 223. He left his son in the care of his chancellor, Zhuge Liang. Zhuge Liang led expedition after expedition north against Wei, and died in camp at the Wuzhang Plains in 234.

Wei's best general against him was Sima Yi. In 249 Sima Yi seized power in Wei in a coup, and his family never let go. Wei conquered Shu in 263. In 266 Sima Yi's grandson Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to step down and founded the Jin dynasty. Only Wu was still standing.

claims.text: Zhuge Liang scared off Sima Yi's army by sitting on the open gates of an empty city, playing the zither.
claims.note: The "empty fort" trick is in the novel. Its only early source is an anecdote Pei Songzhi quoted and himself thought was nonsense.

claims.text: Guan Yu became a god of war.
claims.note: He was honoured more and more over the centuries, and temples to Lord Guan stand across China and beyond.

claims.text: Liu Bei was a descendant of the Han emperors.
claims.note: He claimed descent from a son of Emperor Jing, who had over a hundred children. Chen Shou records the claim; no one could prove it.

reigns.hook: Sima Yan is emperor of Jin, but the job isn't finished. Across the Yangtze, Wu still has its own emperor, and the Jin are building warships.

reigns.tagline: He glued China back together and handed out the knives
reigns.cameToPower: Pushed the last Wei emperor aside
reigns.previously: Sima Yan forces the last Wei emperor out and founds the Jin.
paragraphs: Sima Yan was the third generation of a family that had spent decades taking Wei apart from the inside. In 266 he simply finished the job and called his dynasty Jin. One rival was left: Wu, down on the Yangtze. In 280 his fleets came down the river, the last Wu ruler gave up, and China had one emperor again for the first time in about 90 years.

Then he relaxed. He cut back the provincial armies, but gave the princes of his own family armies of their own, hoping relatives would be loyal. Peace brought a famous splurge. His harem swelled with Wu's palace women, and two courtiers, Shi Chong and Wang Kai, held a contest to see who could waste more money. Worst of all, his heir was famously slow-witted, and he kept him anyway.
When the emperor died in 290, the throne passed to that son. Behind him stood a tough, ambitious wife, and around him stood a ring of uncles and cousins, each with soldiers.

claims.text: He picked which woman to visit by riding through the harem in a goat cart, and women put salt and bamboo leaves outside their doors to make the goats stop.
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu, written over 350 years later. It's a moral tale about a lazy, lustful ruler as much as a report.

claims.text: Shi Chong smashed Wang Kai's prize coral tree, a gift from the emperor, then offered him a choice of bigger ones.
claims.note: A favourite story in later anecdote collections and the Jin Shu. The wealth contest was real enough; the details are polished.

claims.text: Told the people had no grain to eat, his heir asked, "Why don't they eat meat porridge?"
claims.note: From the Jin Shu, written by a later dynasty that had every reason to make the Jin look foolish.

reigns.hook: A simple-minded emperor, a ruthless empress and a dozen princes with private armies. The Jin is about to tear itself to pieces, and the peoples of the north are watching.

reigns.title: The Jin Falls Apart
reigns.tagline: Eight princes, one capital lost, half a country saved
reigns.reignEnded: General Liu Yu took the throne
reigns.previously: Emperor Wu dies. His slow-witted son becomes emperor.
paragraphs: Emperor Hui (290–307) reigned, but others ruled. His wife Jia Nanfeng had rivals murdered until a prince killed her in 300. By then the War of the Eight Princes (291–306) was tearing the north apart. Princes used northern peoples as hired troops, and those peoples (Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Qiang and Jie) soon fought for themselves. In 311 the Xiongnu state of Han-Zhao took Luoyang and captured Emperor Huai. Chang'an fell in 316.

A Jin prince, Sima Rui, set up again at Jiankang (Nanjing) and became emperor in 318. This Eastern Jin held the south while some sixteen kingdoms rose and fell in the north. Refugees poured south. In 353 Wang Xizhi wrote the Orchid Pavilion Preface, still the most famous piece of Chinese calligraphy. In 383 Fu Jian of Former Qin marched south with a vast army and was routed at the Fei River.
The monk Faxian set off on foot for India in 399 to fetch Buddhist texts. But the Jin court was hollow, run by generals. In 420 one of them, Liu Yu, made the last Jin emperor step down.

claims.text: The captured Emperor Huai was made to serve wine at his captor's banquet before he was killed.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu. The humiliation is well attested in outline; the scene is written for maximum shame.

claims.text: After the Fei River, fleeing soldiers took every gust of wind and every cry of a crane for the enemy closing in.
claims.note: The Jin Shu's account, which became a proverb. The defeat was real; the panic is told with relish by the winning side.

claims.text: Tang Taizong had the original Orchid Pavilion Preface buried with him.
claims.note: A Tang-era tale. The original is lost; what survives are early copies, one of the best in the Palace Museum, Beijing.

reigns.hook: Liu Yu's new Song dynasty holds the south. In the north, a Xianbei clan called the Tuoba is about to swallow every rival. China now has two halves, and they'll stay apart for 160 years.

reigns.title: Northern and Southern Dynasties
reigns.tagline: Two Chinas, giant Buddhas and a monk emperor
reigns.reignEnded: A regent took the Zhou throne
reigns.previously: Liu Yu ends the Jin and founds the Song in the south.
paragraphs: In the south, four short dynasties ruled from Jiankang: Song, Qi, Liang and Chen. In the north the Tuoba Xianbei's Northern Wei had united everything by 439. They were Buddhists on a grand scale, carving giant Buddhas into the cliffs at Yungang. Emperor Xiaowen went further. He moved the capital to Luoyang in 494 and banned Xianbei dress and speech at court. New caves were cut at Longmen.

The south had its own believer. Emperor Wu of Liang (502–549) was so devout that he gave himself to a monastery four times, and each time his ministers paid to get him back. His long reign ended in disaster when the turncoat general Hou Jing seized Jiankang. The old emperor died a prisoner in 549.
In the north, Northern Wei split in two in 534. Northern Zhou conquered Northern Qi in 577. Then a Zhou emperor died young, and his father-in-law Yang Jian became regent for a little boy.

claims.text: Emperor Wu of Liang starved to death as Hou Jing's prisoner.
claims.note: The histories say he was denied food and drink at the end, but he was also in his mid-80s and ill.

claims.text: Bodhidharma, founder of Chan (Zen), met Emperor Wu of Liang and told him all his temple-building earned no merit.
claims.note: This meeting first appears in Chan writings centuries later. Even whether Bodhidharma was one real person is debated.

claims.text: Mulan took her father's place in the army.
claims.note: From the Ballad of Mulan, a northern folk song of this era. There's no evidence she was a real person.

reigns.hook: Yang Jian holds the boy emperor's seal. The north is his. Across the Yangtze, a pleasure-loving Chen emperor writes poems. One of them is about to get a very nasty surprise.

reigns.tagline: He reunited China and was terrified of his wife
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne from a boy
reigns.previously: Regent Yang Jian takes the Northern Zhou throne for himself.
paragraphs: Yang Jian came from a northern noble family of mixed Chinese and Xianbei blood. In 581 he took the throne, founded the Sui and built a new capital, Daxing, beside old Chang'an. In 589 his armies crossed the Yangtze and took the Chen capital. For the first time in nearly 300 years, north and south were one again.

Then he got to work. New law codes, a census, the equal-field system handing out land, and huge granaries against famine. He started recruiting some officials by examination rather than birth, and began the canal works his son would finish. He was stingy, suspicious and tireless.

At home, Empress Dugu was the boss. She also helped persuade him to drop his heir Yang Yong in favour of the second son, Yang Guang, who was careful to look modest. In 604 the emperor fell ill at his summer palace and died.

claims.text: Empress Dugu made him promise to have no children by any other woman.
claims.note: The Sui Shu and Zizhi Tongjian tell it. All his sons were hers, which fits, but the vow itself is a good story.

claims.text: When she had a palace girl he'd slept with killed, he rode off alone into the hills and his ministers had to fetch him back.
claims.note: Told in the Zizhi Tongjian, with the emperor complaining that the Son of Heaven had no freedom.

claims.text: Yang Guang had his father murdered on his sickbed.
claims.note: Some accounts say so, but they come from the Tang, who wanted Yang Guang to look as bad as possible. Others just say illness.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is dead, perhaps helped along. Yang Guang takes the throne with grand plans: a new capital, a canal across China and a war he cannot lose.

reigns.tagline: He dug the Grand Canal and lost everything in Korea
reigns.previously: Emperor Wen dies at his summer palace, perhaps murdered.
paragraphs: Yang Guang thought big. He built a new eastern capital at Luoyang. He drove the Grand Canal through from the Yellow River to the Yangtze between 605 and 611, using vast gangs of forced labour. Then he sailed it, on great dragon-boat progresses south to Jiangdu (Yangzhou), with a flotilla of staggering size.

His downfall was Korea. Three times, in 612, 613 and 614, he sent huge armies against the kingdom of Goguryeo. In 612 an army was cut to pieces at the Salsu River. Conscription and taxes drove the empire to revolt, and rebels sprang up everywhere.

The emperor retreated south to Jiangdu and gave up on the north. In April 618 his own guards, led by Yuwen Huaji, turned on him and strangled him. The Tang who came next gave him the posthumous name Yang, an insult, and made him the model of a bad last emperor.

claims.text: Near the end he looked in a mirror and asked who would cut off such a fine head.
claims.note: Recorded in the Zizhi Tongjian, written centuries later. Perfect deathbed drama, and that's a reason for caution.

claims.text: His dragon-boat flotilla stretched for miles along the canal.
claims.note: The histories describe thousands of boats. The exact size grows in the telling.

claims.text: He was a monster of vanity and cruelty.
claims.note: The image comes from Tang historians. Modern historians note his canal and capital served China for centuries.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead in the south. In the north, his cousin Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, already holds Chang'an. All he needs is a reason to stop pretending.

reigns.tagline: He founded the Tang, then his sons fought over it
reigns.previously: Emperor Yang of Sui is strangled by his guards at Jiangdu.
paragraphs: Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, was the Sui garrison commander at Taiyuan, and Emperor Yang's cousin through their mothers. In 617, with the empire in flames, he rebelled and marched on Chang'an. He put a Sui child on the throne as a puppet, and when news came that Emperor Yang was dead, he proclaimed his own Tang dynasty in June 618.

His sons did much of the fighting, crushing rival warlords one by one. Even his daughter, Princess Pingyang, raised her own army. But the crown prince Li Jiancheng and his brilliant younger brother Li Shimin grew to hate each other.

On 2 July 626, Li Shimin ambushed his brothers Jiancheng and Yuanji at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace and killed them both. Days later the old emperor made Shimin his heir. In September he stepped down and lived on as retired emperor until 635.

claims.text: It was Li Shimin, not his father, who pushed for the rebellion of 617.
claims.note: The official histories say so, but they were written under Li Shimin, who had good reason to play up his own role.

claims.text: Princess Pingyang raised an army of tens of thousands to help her father.
claims.note: The Old Book of Tang records her army; she was later given a military funeral. The exact numbers are less certain.

claims.text: Li Shimin shot his elder brother with his own bow at the Xuanwu Gate.
claims.note: That's the official account. Since the winner controlled the record, the claim that his brothers struck first is suspect.

reigns.hook: Two princes lie dead at the palace gate. The man who killed them is about to become the emperor China remembers as one of its very best.

reigns.tagline: A brother-killer who became the model emperor
reigns.cameToPower: Killed his brothers; father stepped down
reigns.previously: Li Shimin kills his brothers at the Xuanwu Gate. Gaozu steps down.
paragraphs: Li Shimin started with blood on his hands and went on to be one of China's most admired emperors. Part of the trick was listening. Wei Zheng, who had once served his murdered brother, became his conscience and told him off to his face, hundreds of times. When Wei died in 643, the emperor said he had lost the mirror that showed him his faults.

He was a soldier too. In 630 his armies crushed the Eastern Turks, and steppe chiefs hailed him as "Heavenly Khagan". The monk Xuanzang slipped off to India in 629 and came home in 645 to an emperor's welcome. A new law code set the pattern for centuries. His invasion of Goguryeo in 645 failed.
His family was another matter. In 643 his crown prince, Li Chengqian, was caught plotting and deposed. Taizong chose his gentle ninth son, Li Zhi. He died in July 649.

claims.text: Taizong hid a pet hawk in his robe when Wei Zheng came in, and Wei talked so long the bird suffocated.
claims.note: A Tang anecdote, not in the main histories. It sums up their relationship a bit too neatly.

claims.text: Wei Zheng criticised him to his face more than 200 times.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Tang histories, which counted his memorials. Taizong also polished his own image as a listener.

claims.text: He may have been killed by an elixir of long life from an Indian alchemist.
claims.note: The histories say he took such drugs late in life. Whether they killed him is guesswork.

reigns.hook: The new emperor Li Zhi is mild and easily led. And among his late father's concubines, now shaved and sent to a nunnery, is a young woman named Wu Zhao.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who shared his throne with Wu Zhao
reigns.previously: Taizong dies. His mild ninth son Li Zhi takes the throne.
paragraphs: When Taizong died, his young concubines were sent off to a Buddhist convent. One of them, Wu Zhao, did not stay there. Within a few years she was back in the palace as a consort of the new emperor. She rose past Empress Wang and the favourite Consort Xiao, and in 655 Gaozong made her empress. Both rivals were soon dead.

From about 660 the emperor suffered strokes or failing eyesight, and Wu ran government beside him. Courtiers called the pair the "two sages". Abroad, these were the Tang's widest years. Allied with the Korean kingdom of Silla, Tang armies destroyed Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.
Gaozong died at Luoyang in December 683. His son Li Xian became emperor as Zhongzong. Everyone knew who held the real power.

claims.text: Wu smothered her own baby daughter and blamed Empress Wang.
claims.note: Found in later histories, hostile to Wu. The baby's death is likely; the murder is not proven.

claims.text: She had her fallen rivals' hands and feet cut off and threw them into a wine vat.
claims.note: The Tang histories tell it; most historians accept the women were killed but treat the details with caution.

claims.text: Gaozong was too ill to rule from about 660.
claims.note: The histories describe dizziness and failing sight. How much he was sidelined and how much he chose to share power is debated.

reigns.hook: The widow will not retire. Within weeks of becoming emperor her son is deposed. Over the next six years Wu Zhao clears the way for something no Chinese woman has ever done.

reigns.tagline: The only woman ever to be emperor of China
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne from her son
reigns.reignEnded: Forced out by a palace coup
reigns.previously: Wu deposes one son, rules through another, then takes the throne.
paragraphs: After Gaozong died, Wu deposed her son Zhongzong after about six weeks in 684 and made his brother Ruizong a puppet. A revolt led by Xu Jingye was crushed. In 690 she stopped pretending. She took the throne in her own name and called her dynasty Zhou. She was the only woman in Chinese history to reign as emperor.

She ruled by fear and talent. Bronze boxes invited anyone to inform on anyone, and cruel officials like Lai Junchen and Zhou Xing ran the terror. She invented new characters, including one for her own name. She promoted the exams and brought clever outsiders into government. She poured money into Buddhism, including the giant Vairocana Buddha at Longmen.

Old age brought new favourites, the Zhang brothers. In February 705, with Wu about 80, officers stormed the palace, killed the Zhangs and made her give the throne back to Zhongzong. She died that December.

claims.text: Zhou Xing was asked how to make a stubborn suspect talk. "Put him in a jar and heat it," he said. "Please step into the jar," came the reply.
claims.note: A famous anecdote, now a Chinese proverb. Zhou Xing did fall from power, but the scene is too neat.

claims.text: The face of the great Vairocana Buddha at Longmen was modelled on Wu's own.
claims.note: A popular modern story. She did fund the carving with her own money, according to an inscription there.

claims.text: Her stele at the Qianling tomb was left blank.
claims.note: It still stands uninscribed. Why is unknown: modesty, confidence, or a verdict nobody dared write.

reigns.hook: Zhongzong is back and the Tang name restored. But his wife and daughter have watched Wu closely, and they think they could do it too.

reigns.title: Empresses and Princesses
reigns.tagline: Everyone wanted to be the next Wu Zetian
reigns.reignEnded: Ruizong handed over to his son
reigns.previously: Wu Zetian is forced out. Zhongzong is restored.
paragraphs: Zhongzong got his throne back in 705 and the Tang name returned. But he had a forceful wife, Empress Wei, and a spoiled daughter, Princess Anle. Both had watched Wu Zetian, and both wanted the same. Anle even asked to be made heir to the throne. The court filled with their favourites, and offices were openly sold.

In 710 Zhongzong died suddenly. Less than three weeks later his nephew Li Longji, son of Ruizong, struck with his aunt Princess Taiping. Their men stormed the palace and killed Empress Wei and Princess Anle. Ruizong was put back on the throne.
The two winners soon fell out. Taiping wanted her own puppet; Li Longji wanted power. In 712 a comet appeared, and Ruizong took it as a sign. He handed the throne to his son and stepped back.

claims.text: Princess Anle asked her father to name her "imperial heir daughter", a crown princess.
claims.note: Reported in the Tang histories. No such title had ever existed, and he did not grant it.

claims.text: Empress Wei and Princess Anle poisoned Zhongzong, some say with a cake.
claims.note: The Tang histories say so, but they were written for the side that killed the two women.

reigns.hook: Li Longji is 27 and now emperor. His aunt Taiping still has half the court. Within a year one of them will be dead, and the winner will preside over the Tang's golden age.

reigns.cameToPower: Father stepped down after a comet
reigns.previously: A comet persuades Ruizong to hand the throne to his son Li Longji.
paragraphs: Li Longji had already helped kill one empress to get here. In 713 he ordered his aunt, Princess Taiping, to kill herself, and then settled in for over 40 years. His Kaiyuan era was the high noon of the Tang. Chang'an was one of the biggest cities on earth, full of Persian merchants, monks and Turkic horsemen. Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei were writing poems. The emperor played music himself and trained performers in his Pear Garden.

Then he fell for Yang Guifei, the wife of his own son, Prince Shou. Her cousin Yang Guozhong became chief minister after the long rule of Li Linfu. The frontier armies grew huge, often under foreign-born generals, and in 751 an Abbasid army beat the Tang at Talas in Central Asia. One general, An Lushan, a vast man of Sogdian and Turkic family, charmed his way into court and was even adopted by Yang Guifei.

In December 755 An Lushan rebelled. He took Luoyang and called himself emperor of Yan. Next summer the old emperor fled west towards Sichuan. At Mawei the guards killed Yang Guozhong and demanded Yang Guifei too. She was strangled. Soon after, at Lingwu, his son made himself emperor without asking. Xuanzong lived on as retired emperor until 762. Bai Juyi's Song of Everlasting Sorrow later turned it all into a love story.

claims.text: Relay riders raced fresh lychees from the far south for Yang Guifei.
claims.note: The Tang histories and Du Mu's poem tell it. Scholars argue over whether the fruit came from distant Lingnan or nearer Sichuan.

claims.text: Yang Guifei had An Lushan bathed and swaddled like a newborn as a palace joke.
claims.note: Told in Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian, written three centuries later, and in gossipy unofficial tales. It may be slander.

claims.text: Chinese prisoners taken at Talas taught the Arabs to make paper.
claims.note: The story appears in later Arabic writings. Paper-making was probably already spreading through Central Asia before 751.

reigns.hook: The old emperor has lost his throne and his love. His son Suzong must now win back two capitals from a rebel army, and he will need foreign help to do it.

reigns.title: Rebellion and Recovery
reigns.tagline: The war that nearly killed the Tang, and the long recovery
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Suzong, Xuanzong's son, and his heirs
reigns.previously: At Mawei, Yang Guifei is strangled. Suzong takes the throne at Lingwu.
paragraphs: Suzong had a throne but no capital. He rebuilt an army with Uyghur horsemen and troops from Central Asia, and in 757 took back Chang'an and Luoyang. The rebels tore themselves apart. An Lushan, half blind and raging, was murdered by his own son that year. His general Shi Siming carried on the fight, until his son killed him too. The war finally ended in 763.

The damage was enormous. The census counted about 53 million people before the war and about 17 million after. In 763 Tibetan troops even held Chang'an for a few weeks. To end the fighting, the court let the regional military governors, the jiedushi, keep their armies. Many soon passed them on to their sons like private kingdoms.

Inside the palace, eunuchs took command of the guard armies. Emperor Dezong had to flee his own capital in 783 when troops mutinied. Then came Xianzong (805–820), tough and stubborn, who forced most of the rebel provinces back under the throne. It looked like a Tang revival. In 820 he died suddenly. The court blamed an elixir of immortality. Plenty of people believed his eunuchs had killed him.

claims.text: The war cut China's population from about 53 million to about 17 million.
claims.note: These are census figures. Historians think a collapse in record-keeping explains much of the drop, though the real death toll was still huge.

claims.text: An Lushan was murdered by his son An Qingxu in 757.
claims.note: Both Tang histories record it. An was going blind and had become violently abusive to those around him.

claims.text: Xianzong was murdered by his eunuchs.
claims.note: The official story was an elixir overdose. The Tang histories say the eunuch Chen Hongzhi was suspected, but nobody was punished.

reigns.hook: The revival dies with Xianzong. Now the eunuchs choose who sits on the throne, and they are not shy about getting rid of emperors who cross them.

reigns.title: The Fall of Tang
reigns.tagline: Eunuchs, a salt smuggler and a warlord finish off the Tang
reigns.previously: Xianzong, the last strong Tang emperor, dies suddenly in 820.
paragraphs: After 820 the eunuchs who ran the palace armies made emperors and sometimes unmade them. In 835 Emperor Wenzong backed a plot to wipe them out, the Sweet Dew Incident, named for the bait: a report of magic dew on a palace tree. It went wrong. The eunuchs' troops massacred the plotters and many officials besides. In 845 Emperor Wuzong turned on Buddhism, shutting monasteries and sending monks and nuns back to the fields.

Culture kept going. In 868 a man named Wang Jie paid for a printed Diamond Sutra in honour of his parents. Meanwhile the countryside was boiling. In 875 the salt smuggler Huang Chao rose in revolt. His army marched the length of China, sacked Guangzhou in 879 and took Chang'an in 881, where Huang called himself emperor. It took the Tang and their Shatuo Turk allies until 884 to destroy him.

The real winner was Zhu Wen, one of Huang Chao's officers who had switched sides. In 903 he slaughtered the palace eunuchs. In 904 he hauled the emperor to Luoyang, pulled Chang'an down and had the emperor killed. He put a boy on the throne, then in 907 took it for himself. The Tang, after almost 300 years, was over.

claims.text: Huang Chao's army massacred over 100,000 foreign merchants at Guangzhou.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Arab writer Abu Zayd of Siraf. No Chinese source gives it, and it may be inflated.

claims.text: Wuzong's purge closed over 4,600 monasteries.
claims.note: The number comes from the emperor's own edict of 845, which may round up for effect. The purge itself was real and huge.

claims.text: The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.
claims.note: Found in the sealed library cave at Dunhuang and now in the British Library. Its colophon gives the date.

reigns.hook: Zhu Wen has his own dynasty. But the empire has shattered, and in the north five dynasties will rise and fall in barely half a century.

reigns.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
reigns.tagline: Five dynasties in 53 years, and a deal with the Khitans
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Zhu Wen, Tang general turned usurper
reigns.cameToPower: Zhu Wen forced the Tang out
reigns.reignEnded: A general took the boy's throne
reigns.previously: Zhu Wen forces the last Tang boy emperor to abdicate in 907.
paragraphs: North China now went through five dynasties in 53 years: Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou. Zhu Wen's Later Liang lasted until 923, though he was murdered by his own son in 912. In the south about ten kingdoms got on with life, trading, building and painting in comfort. Beyond the northern frontier, the Khitan leader Abaoji founded a new empire, the Liao, in 916.

In 936 Shi Jingtang wanted the throne and bought Khitan help with the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing. He even called himself 'son emperor' to a Khitan ruler younger than he was. Those prefectures would haunt Chinese rulers for centuries. In 947 the Khitans turned on his heir and sacked Kaifeng. Through it all the minister Feng Dao served five dynasties and ten emperors, and found time to have the Confucian classics printed.

Then came Chai Rong, Shizong of Later Zhou, who rebuilt the army into the best fighting force in decades. He beat the Southern Tang and won back ground from the Liao. In 959 he died suddenly, leaving a six-year-old son. His palace commander, a tough cavalry officer named Zhao Kuangyin, had the army behind him.

claims.text: Shi Jingtang called the Khitan emperor 'father', though he was ten years older.
claims.note: Recorded in the Old and New Histories of the Five Dynasties; the age gap comes from their recorded birth years.

claims.text: Feng Dao sponsored the first printed edition of the Confucian classics.
claims.note: The printing at the Directorate of Education ran from 932 to 953 and is well recorded, though no copy survives.

claims.text: The Night Revels of Han Xizai began as a spy's report: the Southern Tang ruler sent a painter to see how his minister partied.
claims.note: The tale is told in Song writings about painting. The surviving scroll is a later copy, so it can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Shizong's little son sits on the throne. His army has other ideas. On a cold morning at Chenqiao, the officers throw a yellow robe over their commander.

reigns.tagline: The general who got crowned in his own army camp
reigns.previously: Shizong of Later Zhou dies, leaving a boy of six on the throne.
paragraphs: Early in 960 Zhao Kuangyin marched out of Kaifeng to meet a reported Khitan attack. At Chenqiao, a day's march away, his officers woke him, threw a yellow imperial robe over his shoulders and hailed him emperor. He turned round, took the capital almost without a fight and named his dynasty Song. He treated the boy emperor and his family kindly, which was rare for the time.

Zhao knew what killed dynasties: generals. So in 961, the story goes, he threw a banquet for his top commanders and told them over wine he couldn't sleep for fear one of them would get a yellow robe too. They took the hint, retired to rich estates and gave up their armies. For the rest of the dynasty, scholar-officials outranked soldiers. He picked off the south: Later Shu in 965, Southern Han in 971, Southern Tang in 975, whose last ruler was the poet Li Yu.

He never got the Sixteen Prefectures back from the Liao. In November 976 he died suddenly at 49. His younger brother Zhao Kuangyi had been with him that night, and it was the brother, not one of his sons, who took the throne.

claims.text: Zhao was taken by surprise when his officers made him emperor.
claims.note: Song histories tell it that way, but the robe was ready and the plan ran smoothly. Most historians think he and his brother set it up.

claims.text: Taizu talked his generals into retirement over a cup of wine.
claims.note: The scene appears in Song accounts written decades later. The generals did lose their commands, but probably over years, not at one banquet.

claims.text: 'Candle shadows and the sound of an axe': Taizu was killed by his brother.
claims.note: A monk's account from the next century describes shadows and an axe that night. Nothing proves murder, but the brother's quick takeover fed suspicion for centuries.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is Taizu's brother, Taizong. He wants to finish the conquest, but the Khitan cavalry of the Liao are waiting in the north.

reigns.title: Peace with the Khitans
reigns.tagline: Silver for peace, and a century of quiet brilliance
reigns.previously: Taizu dies suddenly in the night. His brother takes the throne.
paragraphs: Taizong conquered Northern Han in 979, the last holdout in the north, then went for the Sixteen Prefectures. At the Gaoliang River near modern Beijing, the Liao routed his army. The Liao struck back deep into Song land in 1004, and the next year his son Zhenzong (997–1022) agreed the Treaty of Chanyuan: 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year, in return for peace.

It worked. The border stayed quiet for over a century. Zhenzong cheered himself up with 'heavenly texts' that conveniently dropped from the sky in 1008. Renzong reigned from 1022 to 1063, at first under the Empress Dowager Liu. The Tangut Western Xia declared their own empire in 1038 and years of costly war followed. Fan Zhongyan's reforms of 1043 lasted barely two years.

Still, these were brilliant times. The exams turned scholar-officials into the ruling class. Ouyang Xiu wrote history and essays, and the upright judge Bao Zheng became the hero of countless later plays. A commoner named Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay. Renzong had no surviving son, so a cousin's son, Yingzong, reigned briefly from 1063 to 1067.

claims.text: Taizong fled the Gaoliang River in a donkey cart with an arrow wound.
claims.note: The detail comes from later accounts. The official Song record says little about the rout, so the colour is hard to check.

claims.text: Under the Treaty of Chanyuan the Song paid the Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year.
claims.note: The terms are recorded in both Song and Liao sources. The payments were raised in 1042.

claims.text: Bi Sheng invented movable type in the 1040s.
claims.note: Known only from Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays, written a few decades later. None of Bi Sheng's type survives.

reigns.hook: In 1067 a teenager takes the throne. Shenzong thinks the empire is broke and its army is a joke, and he has found a minister who agrees.

reigns.tagline: The young emperor who bet everything on reform
reigns.previously: Yingzong dies after four years. His teenage son takes over.
paragraphs: Shenzong came to the throne set on fixing two things: an empty treasury and an army that kept losing. In 1069 he handed power to Wang Anshi, a brilliant, stubborn official with a plan. The New Policies poured out: cheap state loans to farmers at planting time, called the 'green sprouts'; village militias; state trading; new ways to collect tax. Wang wanted the state to grow the economy and then tax the growth.

Half the court hated it. Sima Guang led the opposition, then retired to Luoyang, where he finished his giant history, the Zizhi Tongjian, in 1084. The poet Su Shi mocked the reforms in verse, was put on trial by the Censorate, the 'Crow Terrace', in 1079, and sent into exile. Wang Anshi left office for good in 1076, but Shenzong kept many of his policies.

He wanted a war too. The campaigns against the Western Xia went badly, and in 1082 the new fortress of Yongle fell with terrible losses. Meanwhile the polymath Shen Kuo wrote down how a magnetised needle points south. Shenzong died in 1085, aged about 36. His son was a small boy, so Shenzong's mother, the Empress Dowager Gao, took charge and called Sima Guang back.

claims.text: Su Shi was put on trial for poems mocking the reforms.
claims.note: The Crow Terrace case of 1079 is well documented. He escaped with exile to Huangzhou.

claims.text: Shen Kuo gave the first clear description of the magnetic compass needle.
claims.note: His Dream Pool Essays (about 1088) are the earliest clear account of a magnetised needle used to find direction.

claims.text: The New Policies ruined ordinary farmers.
claims.note: That was the opponents' charge, repeated by later Confucian historians. Modern historians see a mixed record, with real gains for the treasury.

reigns.hook: Shenzong's son Zhezong is a boy, and the regent undoes the reforms. When he grows up he brings them back, then dies young. The throne passes to his brother, an artist.

reigns.title: Huizong and the Fall of Kaifeng
reigns.tagline: The artist emperor who painted while his empire fell
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of Zhezong; Qinzong his son
reigns.reignEnded: Both carried off by the Jurchens
reigns.previously: Zhezong revives his father's reforms, then dies young without a son.
paragraphs: Huizong was one of the finest artists ever to sit on a throne. He painted birds and flowers with uncanny precision and invented his own elegant 'slender gold' calligraphy. His Auspicious Cranes scroll shows birds wheeling over a palace gate. He loved Daoism, collected rare rocks and plants, and left government to the minister Cai Jing. Kaifeng was rich, crowded and busy, like the scene in the scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival.

The convoys hauling rocks for his gardens, the Huashigang, squeezed the south-east and helped spark Fang La's huge rebellion in 1120. An outlaw named Song Jiang raided in the north, the seed of the later novel Water Margin. Then Huizong made his big mistake. In 1120 he allied with the Jurchens, whose new Jin empire was tearing apart the Liao. The Liao fell in 1125, and the Jin, having seen how feeble Song armies were, turned on the Song.

In January 1126 Huizong panicked and handed the throne to his son Qinzong. It didn't help. Kaifeng fell in January 1127. In the Jingkang Incident both emperors, thousands of the imperial clan and much of the court were marched north as prisoners. Huizong died in captivity in the far north-east in 1135. Qinzong lived on as a captive until around 1156.

claims.text: Huizong painted the Auspicious Cranes himself.
claims.note: It carries his inscription, but many 'Huizong' paintings were made by his court academy artists, and scholars argue over which are his own.

claims.text: Along the River During the Qingming Festival shows Kaifeng in Huizong's time.
claims.note: The scroll is attributed to Zhang Zeduan and usually dated to the early 12th century, but some scholars date it later or doubt it shows Kaifeng at all.

claims.text: Huizong died a prisoner of the Jin in 1135.
claims.note: Song and Jin records agree. His coffin was sent back to the Southern Song under the peace of 1141.

reigns.hook: Every prince in Kaifeng has been taken north. Every prince but one. Huizong's ninth son, Prince Kang, was away from the city, and now he is the dynasty's last hope.

reigns.tagline: The prince who got away, and the general he let die
reigns.cameToPower: Only prince to escape the Jin
reigns.previously: Kaifeng falls. Huizong, Qinzong and the court are marched north.
paragraphs: Prince Kang had been sent out of Kaifeng on a mission and missed the disaster. In June 1127 he was crowned at Yingtian, today's Shangqiu. The Jin came after him fast. Their general Wuzhu chased him over the Yangtze, and the emperor fled to sea, riding out the winter of 1129–1130 on ships off the coast. On its way back north, the Jin fleet was trapped at Huangtiandang by the general Han Shizhong.

Gaozong settled at Lin'an, today's Hangzhou. This was the Southern Song. In 1140 his best general, Yue Fei, was winning battles and pushing towards the old capital when he was ordered back. Gaozong and his chancellor Qin Hui wanted peace with the Jin. The Treaty of Shaoxing in 1141 made the Song a vassal of the Jin, with the border on the Huai River.

Yue Fei was arrested and killed in prison in January 1142. Asked for proof of his treason, Qin Hui is said to have answered: 'Perhaps there was something.' Iron statues of Qin Hui, his wife and two accomplices still kneel at Yue Fei's tomb in Hangzhou. Gaozong had no surviving son. In 1162 he handed the throne to his adopted heir, a descendant of Taizu, and lived on in comfort until 1187.

claims.text: Yue Fei was recalled by twelve gold-lacquered orders in a single day.
claims.note: The story comes from Song accounts sympathetic to Yue Fei, many gathered by his grandson Yue Ke. The number may be dramatised.

claims.text: Yue Fei's mother tattooed 'serve the country with utmost loyalty' on his back.
claims.note: The Song Shi says words like these were on his back at his trial. The scene with his mother is a much later addition from fiction and opera.

claims.text: Gaozong let Yue Fei die because victory might bring his brother Qinzong home to reclaim the throne.
claims.note: A popular explanation since the Ming. Historians point out that Gaozong also shared the old Song fear of over-mighty generals.

reigns.hook: Gaozong hands over to Xiaozong, who dreams of retaking the north. Instead the Southern Song will grow rich, until a new enemy rides in from the steppe.

reigns.title: The Southern Song
reigns.tagline: A dazzling empire in the south, and a boy lost to the sea
reigns.reignEnded: Last boy emperor drowned at Yamen
reigns.previously: Gaozong steps down, handing the throne to his adopted son Xiaozong.
paragraphs: Xiaozong (1162–1189) tried to win back the north, failed, and settled for the Longxing peace with the Jin in 1164. After that the Southern Song got rich. Hangzhou grew into a vast, glittering city, the 'Quinsay' Marco Polo later raved about. Rice, porcelain and silk poured out, sea trade boomed and paper money changed hands. Zhu Xi built the Neo-Confucian philosophy that would shape the exams for 600 years.

Then the Mongols came. Genghis Khan took the Jin capital Zhongdu, now Beijing, in 1215. The Song helped finish off the Jin in 1234, then tried to grab Kaifeng and Luoyang and were thrown out. War with the Mongols followed. In 1259 the Great Khan Möngke died besieging the Song fortress of Diaoyu. His brother Kublai hurried off to claim the throne, and the Song got a breather under the chancellor Jia Sidao.

It didn't last. Xiangyang held out from 1268 to 1273, until Persian engineers built counterweight trebuchets that hurled huge stones into it. In 1276 Lin'an surrendered with the boy emperor and his grandmother. Loyalists fled south with two more child princes. At Yamen on 19 March 1279 the Mongol fleet won, and the minister Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the last emperor, the child Zhao Bing, on his back.

claims.text: Hangzhou was the largest city in the world, with over a million people.
claims.note: Estimates rest on Song local records and Marco Polo's dazzled account. Modern figures vary widely.

claims.text: Möngke was killed by a Song missile at Diaoyu.
claims.note: Some Chinese accounts hint at a wound. The Persian historian Rashid al-Din says he died of dysentery, and disease is the likelier cause.

claims.text: Lu Xiufu drowned himself with the boy emperor on his back.
claims.note: The Song Shi records it. The more dramatic details, such as crowds of courtiers following them into the sea, come from loyalist tradition.

reigns.hook: The Song is gone. For the first time all of China belongs to a conqueror from outside: Kublai, grandson of Genghis Khan, who has ruled his own Chinese-style dynasty, the Yuan, since 1271.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of the Great Khan Möngke
reigns.previously: The Song are drowned at Yamen. Now, the man who beat them.
paragraphs: Kublai was a grandson of Genghis Khan, but he grew up curious about the settled farming world his grandfather had smashed. When his brother, the Great Khan Möngke, died in 1259, Kublai had himself elected khan at Kaiping, his summer capital, the Xanadu of later poems. His younger brother Ariq Böke claimed the title too. Kublai won the four-year civil war, but the wider Mongol empire never truly obeyed one khan again.

He built a new capital, Dadu, where Beijing stands today, and in 1271 named his dynasty Yuan. Once the Song fell in 1279 it became the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China. He ran on paper money, pushed the Grand Canal up to his capital and had the Tibetan lama 'Phags-pa design a new script. Subjects were ranked: Mongols first, southern Chinese last. The captured Song minister Wen Tianxiang refused every offer and was executed in 1283.

Japan was the one that got away. Invasion fleets sailed in 1274 and 1281, and the second was wrecked by a typhoon the Japanese called kamikaze, the divine wind. At home Kublai lost his beloved wife Chabi in 1281 and his heir Zhenjin in 1285. He ate and drank too much, suffered badly from gout, and died in 1294 aged 78. The throne went to Zhenjin's son Temür.

claims.text: Marco Polo served Kublai for 17 years as a trusted official.
claims.note: Polo's book is the only source. No Chinese record names him, so some scholars doubt his role, though many of his details about Yuan China ring true.

claims.text: A typhoon destroyed the 1281 invasion fleet off Japan.
claims.note: Japanese and Chinese records agree on the storm. The size of the fleet, often given as over 4,000 ships, is probably inflated.

claims.text: The four-class ranking of Mongols, semu, northern and southern Chinese was a rigid caste system.
claims.note: The ranking was real in appointments and some laws, but historians argue it was applied unevenly and never set out as one formal code.

reigns.hook: Kublai has outlived his son. His grandson Temür inherits the richest empire on earth, and a family that is about to start killing each other for it.

reigns.title: The Last Mongol Emperors
reigns.tagline: Nine emperors, one flood and a beggar monk with an army
reigns.previously: Kublai Khan dies at Dadu. His grandson Temür inherits.
paragraphs: Temür ruled steadily from 1294 to 1307. After him the wheels came off. About nine emperors came and went in 26 years, through coups, poisonings and a civil war. The young reformer Shidebala was murdered in a coup in 1323. There was one bright spot: Ayurbarwada, a cultured emperor who read Chinese, brought back the civil service exams, held again in 1315 for the first time under the Yuan.

The last Yuan emperor in China, Toghon Temür, took the throne as a boy in 1333. His able minister Toghto tried to fix things, and in 1351 he sent a vast workforce to repair the Yellow River dykes after the floods of 1344. The work camps became a breeding ground for revolt. The Red Turbans, followers of the White Lotus sect, rose that same year. Paper money collapsed and the south split into rival rebel states.

Out of the chaos climbed Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphaned peasant who had been a monk and a beggar before joining Guo Zixing's rebel army. He crushed his great rival Chen Youliang on Lake Poyang in 1363, took the rest of the south, and on 23 January 1368 proclaimed the Ming at Nanjing. That September his troops entered Dadu. Toghon Temür fled to the steppe, where his heirs carried on as the Northern Yuan.

claims.text: Rebels dug up a one-eyed stone man in the Yellow River works, carved with a prophecy that it would set the empire in revolt.
claims.note: Told in accounts of the Red Turban rising. If the statue existed at all, rebel leaders most likely buried it there to be found.

claims.text: Lake Poyang in 1363 was one of the largest naval battles in history.
claims.note: The Ming histories give hundreds of thousands of men on each side. Historians accept it was huge but doubt the exact figures.

claims.text: Ayurbarwada brought back the civil service exams, held in 1315.
claims.note: Recorded in the Yuan Shi. Quotas and easier papers favoured Mongol and Central Asian candidates.

reigns.hook: A beggar monk now sits on the throne at Nanjing. He remembers having no land to bury his parents in, and he trusts nobody with power.

reigns.tagline: From begging bowl to the dragon throne
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rebel who drove out the Yuan
reigns.previously: The Mongols flee Dadu. A peasant rebel has founded the Ming.
paragraphs: Zhu Yuanzhang was born dirt poor. In 1344 famine and plague killed his parents and eldest brother within weeks, and he later wrote that the family had no land to bury them in. He became a novice monk, begged on the roads, then joined the rebels. Twenty-four years later he was emperor. He ruled from Nanjing as the Hongwu Emperor, with Empress Ma at his side, remembered by the histories as brave and kind.

He rebuilt the countryside with land surveys and the Yellow Registers, which listed every household for tax and labour. But he was ferociously suspicious. In 1380 he had his chancellor Hu Weiyong executed for treason, abolished the post for good and ran the government himself. The purge rolled on for years, and another hit the general Lan Yu in 1393. His secret police, the Embroidered Uniform Guard, made the arrests, and officials were flogged in open court.

His heir, Zhu Biao, died in 1392. Hongwu passed over his own grown sons and named Zhu Biao's teenage son, Zhu Yunwen. When the old emperor died in June 1398, the young man became the Jianwen Emperor, with a ring of powerful uncles watching him.

claims.text: The Hu Weiyong purge killed about 30,000 people.
claims.note: The figure comes from Ming records and later histories and covers executions spread over more than a decade. It can't be checked precisely.

claims.text: Empress Ma had big, unbound feet.
claims.note: A popular tradition that fits her humble origins and her bold character. It comes from later stories, not from her official biography.

claims.text: Hongwu's ugly portraits show his real face, and the handsome ones were painted to flatter him.
claims.note: Both types survive. Why there are two is unknown; the tale that he punished honest painters is a later story with no solid evidence.

reigns.hook: Jianwen's advisers want to cut his uncles down to size. The toughest uncle, the Prince of Yan, sits in Beijing with a battle-hardened army.

reigns.tagline: He stole his nephew's throne, then built the Forbidden City
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Uncle of Jianwen; son of Hongwu
reigns.previously: The Hongwu Emperor dies. His grandson Jianwen takes the throne.
paragraphs: The young Jianwen Emperor began stripping his uncles of their princedoms. In 1399 the eldest surviving one, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, rebelled from Beijing. After three years of war he took Nanjing in July 1402. The palace went up in flames and Jianwen vanished. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor and punished anyone who had stayed loyal. The scholar Fang Xiaoru refused to draft his proclamation and was executed along with hundreds of his relatives.

Then he went big. The eunuch admiral Zheng He led huge fleets to South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, seven voyages between 1405 and 1433. In 1414 a giraffe from East Africa reached the court and was hailed as a qilin, a lucky beast of legend. Scholars compiled the Yongle Encyclopedia, over 11,000 volumes. His armies invaded Vietnam in 1407. And he moved the capital to Beijing, where the new Forbidden City was ready in 1421.

He led five campaigns into Mongolia in person. Coming home from the last one, in August 1424, he died in the field aged 64. His son, a heavy, bookish man, took the throne and began cancelling his father's costly schemes.

claims.text: The Jianwen Emperor escaped the burning palace disguised as a monk.
claims.note: The official line was that he died in the fire, but no body was clearly identified. The Ming Shi says rumours of his escape were one reason Zheng He's fleets were sent out.

claims.text: Fang Xiaoru's family was wiped out to the 'ten degrees', 873 people in all.
claims.note: Later accounts give totals in the hundreds, often 873. Adding his students as a tenth 'degree' of kin may be a later embellishment.

claims.text: A giraffe brought to the court in 1414 was hailed as a qilin.
claims.note: A court painting of the animal with the official Shen Du's poem of praise survives in a later copy.

reigns.hook: Yongle dies on the steppe. His heirs will send the treasure fleets out once more, then a boy emperor and his favourite eunuch will march an army into disaster.

reigns.title: Tumu and the Captive Emperor
reigns.tagline: The emperor who rode out to war and came back a prisoner
reigns.previously: The Yongle Emperor dies on his way home from Mongolia.
paragraphs: Yongle's son, the Hongxi Emperor, lasted ten months. His son Xuande (1425–1435) was a capable ruler and a gifted painter. He sent Zheng He on one last voyage in 1431, and after the fleet came home in 1433 the treasure ships never sailed again. Then a boy took the throne: the Zhengtong Emperor, aged seven, who grew up devoted to his eunuch tutor Wang Zhen.

In 1449 the Oirat Mongol leader Esen raided the frontier. Wang Zhen talked the 21-year-old emperor into leading an army out himself. It was a shambles. At Tumu, in September 1449, the army was destroyed, Wang Zhen was killed and the emperor was taken prisoner. In Beijing the minister Yu Qian refused to flee, put the emperor's brother on the throne as the Jingtai Emperor, and held the city.

Esen sent the captive home in 1450, and Jingtai kept him locked up for seven years. In 1457, with Jingtai ill, a coup put him back on the throne as the Tianshun Emperor, and Yu Qian, who had saved the dynasty, was executed. Dying in 1464, Tianshun banned burying palace women alive with emperors. Then came Chenghua, ruled by his much older consort Lady Wan, and the steady Hongzhi Emperor (1487–1505).

claims.text: Lady Wan, about 17 years older than the Chenghua Emperor, had other consorts' babies killed, so his heir was raised in hiding.
claims.note: The story is in the Ming Shi and later accounts. The tale of the boy kept secret until he was five may well be dramatised.

claims.text: The Hongzhi Emperor had only one wife, Empress Zhang.
claims.note: The records list no other consorts, which made him unique among Ming emperors.

claims.text: Xuande was a passionate fan of cricket fighting.
claims.note: Later Ming anecdotes say so, and fine cricket jars were made in his reign, but the court records are quiet about it.

reigns.hook: Hongzhi dies in 1505 with one son. That son, the Zhengde Emperor, has no intention whatsoever of being a model ruler.

reigns.title: The Playboy and the Daoist
reigns.tagline: One emperor partied, the next one chased immortality
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Only son of the Hongzhi Emperor
reigns.previously: The steady Hongzhi Emperor dies, leaving his only son.
paragraphs: The Zhengde Emperor (1505–1521) treated the throne like a playground. He built a pleasure palace, the Leopard Quarter, kept wild animals, roamed in disguise and gave himself a general's rank under a made-up name. His eunuch Liu Jin ran the government until 1510, when he was arrested and executed by slicing. When the Prince of Ning rebelled in 1519, the philosopher-general Wang Yangming beat him before the emperor could even arrive.

In 1520 Zhengde fell out of a boat while fishing, fell ill and died the next spring without a son. His teenage cousin became the Jiajing Emperor (1521–1567) and at once picked a fight over honouring his own father as an emperor. Officials who protested at the palace gate in 1524 were flogged, and some died. Jiajing grew obsessed with Daoist rites and elixirs. In 1542 palace women tried to strangle him in his sleep, but the knot slipped.

After that he barely met his ministers. Altan Khan's Mongols reached the walls of Beijing in 1550, and pirates raided the coast until generals like Qi Jiguang beat them. The official Hai Rui sent a memorial telling the emperor bluntly that he was failing his people. Jiajing died in 1567. His son Longqing (1567–1572) opened a port to private overseas trade and made peace with Altan Khan in 1571.

claims.text: Palace women tried to strangle the Jiajing Emperor in his bed in 1542.
claims.note: The plot is in the court records. The women and two consorts accused with them were executed by slicing.

claims.text: Hai Rui bought his own coffin before sending his memorial, expecting to die for it.
claims.note: The story is told in his official biography, which may have polished it to make him a model of courage.

claims.text: Jiajing was killed by his Daoist elixirs.
claims.note: His last illness fits poisoning by the mercury and arsenic in such elixirs, but the cause can't be proved.

reigns.hook: Longqing dies in 1572 and the throne goes to a little boy. Standing behind him is a grand secretary who means to run the empire hard.
